lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 6, what are the four steps for looking at art? (Describe, analyse, interpret and judge.) Today: choosing your best work and showing it.
A portfolio is a collection of your work that shows what you can do and how you have grown. Curating means choosing it and arranging it, as a museum's curator does.
Choose your strongest pieces and a range of materials and ideas. Add a few that show progress, such as a first sketch beside the finished piece. Fewer, better pieces beat many.
Arrange them by theme, by technique or by date, so they tell a story. Photograph flat work in even daylight, straight on, then crop the edges.
Label each piece as a gallery does: its title, the year, the materials and the size, for example: Stormy Harbour, 2026, pencil and watercolour, 30 × 21 cm.
An artist's statement is a short paragraph in your own words: what the work is about, how you made it and why. Write I, keep it clear, and say what you hope viewers notice.
Hang the work with the centres of the pictures on one line, about 1.5 m from the floor, at eye level. Leave even gaps. Ask for feedback that is kind, specific and helpful, and give it that way too.
Try it in the world: choose your best 5 pieces from this year, photograph and label them, and write a 3-sentence statement about one. Next: in grade 8, Impressionism and light.

exercises.prompt: What does curating a portfolio mean?
exercises.hint: Think of what a museum's curator does.
choices: choosing and arranging work to show it
exercises.explain: Curating is choosing the right pieces and arranging them to tell a story.

exercises.prompt: A few strong pieces are better than every piece you have ever made.
exercises.hint: Would a viewer look at 200 drawings?
exercises.explain: True: choose the strongest few, and each gets the attention it deserves.

exercises.prompt: What belongs on a gallery label?
exercises.hint: A label tells viewers about the work.
exercises.explain: Its title, the year, the materials and the size.

exercises.prompt: At about what height are the centres of pictures hung?
exercises.hint: Where are a grown-up's eyes when standing?
exercises.explain: About 1.5 m from the floor, at eye level.

exercises.prompt: Sort the feedback into helpful and not helpful.
items: The dark sky makes the boat stand out.
Try a lighter blue in the distance.
The hands look stiff: try gesture sketches.
exercises.hint: Helpful feedback says exactly what works or what to try.
exercises.explain: Specific comments help; I don't like it and Nice do not say what or why.

exercises.hint: Look for one line through the pictures' centres.
exercises.explain: The first: the centres are on one line at eye level, with even gaps.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence belongs in an artist's statement?
exercises.hint: A statement says what, how and why, in your own voice.
choices: I used cool blues to make the harbour calm.
This is the best painting ever made.
My friend did most of it.
exercises.explain: I used cool blues to make the harbour calm: it says what you did and why.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of making a portfolio in order.
exercises.hint: You cannot choose before you gather.
exercises.explain: Gather, choose, arrange and label, then write the statement.

exercises.prompt: How should you photograph a flat drawing?
choices: in even daylight, straight on, then crop
with a flash, at an angle
exercises.explain: Even daylight, straight on, then crop it neatly.

exercises.prompt: A first sketch can be worth showing beside the finished piece.
exercises.hint: What does it show about how you work?
exercises.explain: True: it shows how your idea grew.

exercises.prompt: Match each part of a label to an example.
exercises.hint: Which is a name, a date, what it is made with, and how big?
exercises.explain: Title: Stormy Harbour; year: 2026; materials: pencil and watercolour; size: 30 × 21 cm.

exercises.prompt: Feedback should be kind, specific and helpful.
exercises.hint: Think of feedback you would like to get.

exercises.prompt: Which is the most helpful feedback?
exercises.hint: Which says exactly what works and what to try?
choices: The shadows are strong; the face needs one too.
I would have drawn a dog.
exercises.explain: It names what works (the shadows) and what to try next (a shadow on the face).

exercises.prompt: A portfolio has 20 drawings of cats. What would make it stronger?
exercises.hint: A portfolio shows your range as well as your best.
choices: the best few, plus other subjects and materials
make them all the same size
exercises.explain: Choose the best few cats, and show other subjects and materials too.

exercises.prompt: A wall is 5 m wide. Three pictures, each 1 m wide, hang with equal gaps at both ends and between them. How wide is each gap?
exercises.hint: How much wall is left? How many gaps are there?
exercises.explain: 5 − 3 = 2 m is left, shared between 4 gaps: 2 ÷ 4 = 0.5 m.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is in the artist's own voice?
choices: I wanted the storm to feel close.
exercises.explain: I wanted the storm to feel close: in the first person, about the work.

exercises.prompt: Sort them: does it belong on a gallery label?
exercises.hint: A label tells the viewer about the work itself.
exercises.explain: On the label: the title, the year, the materials and the size. Not on it: your home address is private, and the price of your paints tells the viewer nothing about the work.

exercises.prompt: Pictures are hung with their centres 150 cm from the floor. A picture is 60 cm tall. How high is its top edge from the floor, in cm?
exercises.hint: The centre is halfway up the picture. How far above the centre is the top?
exercises.explain: Half of 60 cm is 30 cm, so the top is 30 cm above the centre. 150 + 30 = 180 cm from the floor.
